strengths: The paper addresses a timely and relevant NLP/agent-systems problem: scalable tool and agent routing under large MCP-style candidate spaces, where static prompt injection and simple embedding retrieval are plausible bottlenecks.

The proposed pipeline is coherent: graph-based candidate expansion, synthetic multi-turn trajectory generation, supervised fine-tuning of a history-aware router, and a lightweight routing-agent wrapper form a clear end-to-end approach.

Empirical comparisons are broad, including embedding retrieval, ReAct, open and closed LLM routers, and evaluations on MCP-Universe and MCP-Mark. The reported gains of the 8B router over much larger generalist LLMs are promising.
The paper includes useful stress tests for large candidate pools and noisy candidate additions, plus an ablation showing that history improves routing accuracy over a query-only variant.
The writing is generally understandable, and the appendix provides mutation taxonomies and representative prompts/examples that help clarify the synthetic data construction.
weaknesses: The central claims about generalization to the Agent Web and multi-agent orchestration are stronger than the evidence supports. The agent-routing benchmark appears constructed by the authors with only 156 samples, using similar mutation/synthesis machinery to the training pipeline, so it is unclear whether the 91.6% accuracy reflects real cross-domain transfer rather than benchmark-generation alignment.

Reproducibility is limited. Key details are missing or underspecified, including the exact train/test splits, candidate pools, generated datasets, trajectory synthesis prompts beyond mutation prompts, random-walk parameters, filtering/validation procedures for synthetic labels, and whether code/data will be released. Dependence on GPT-4o-generated supervision also complicates reproduction.

The evaluation evidence is somewhat fragile. MCP-Mark appears very small, with domain scores moving in 10-point increments, yet the paper reports no confidence intervals, standard deviations, or significance tests despite using avg@5. Some claimed improvements may not be statistically reliable.

The paper does not sufficiently rule out leakage or circularity. Mutation-derived candidates are used for training and also for robustness testing, and the agent benchmark is generated using the same broad design principles, raising concerns that the router is being evaluated on distributions too close to its synthetic supervision.

The baselines are not always described in enough detail for fairness. It is unclear how prompts were constructed for closed-source LLM routers, how candidate descriptions/history were provided under context constraints, whether all models saw equivalent information, and how parsing failures or invalid outputs were handled.

The method’s novelty is moderate rather than decisive: graph expansion, LLM-generated synthetic tool-use trajectories, and supervised router fine-tuning are sensible combinations of existing ideas. The main contribution is engineering and empirical packaging, but the paper sometimes presents this as a broader foundational paradigm.

The actual downstream task success is conflated with routing accuracy in places. Since execution is fixed to Gemini-2.5-Pro, the paper should more clearly isolate when it measures exact route selection versus end-to-end task completion, and how gold tools/agents are defined for multi-step tasks.

Several claims are overgeneralized, such as scaling to web-scale open ecosystems and universal orchestration. The largest reported tool bank is only about 2,005 tools, which is useful but not enough to substantiate those broader scalability claims.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and relevant NLP/agent-systems problem: routing among large and growing MCP tool or agent spaces, where static prompt injection and simple embedding retrieval are plausible bottlenecks.

The proposed pipeline is coherent at a high level: candidate-graph construction, mutation-based expansion, synthetic multi-turn trajectory generation, and fine-tuning a lightweight history-aware router are natural components for this task.
The experiments compare against several reasonable families of baselines, including embedding retrieval, ReAct-style routing, open-source models, and closed-source LLM routers.
The reported gains are consistent across the main tables, especially on MCP-Mark and in noisy candidate settings, suggesting that a specialized router may indeed be useful for tool selection.
The paper includes some implementation details, such as base model, LoRA setup, sequence length, learning rate, batch size, embedding model, and synthesis model.
weaknesses: The central empirical claims are much stronger than the evidence supports. The paper repeatedly claims scalability to the Agent Web, universal orchestration, and robust web-scale routing, but the actual evaluation uses modest candidate pools, easy-mode MCP-Mark, and a small 156-example author-constructed agent-routing benchmark.

There is a serious risk of evaluation leakage or self-confirming evaluation. The training tool bank is collected from MCP-Universe and LiveMCP, while evaluation is also on MCP-Universe/MCP-Mark-like tool spaces; the paper does not clearly define held-out tools, held-out servers, held-out tasks, or how synthetic training samples are prevented from matching benchmark labels.

The agent-routing generalization result is especially weak: the benchmark is constructed by the authors using their own normalization/mutation/synthesis pipeline, has only 156 samples, and appears closely aligned with the training prompt format. This does not convincingly demonstrate transfer from tool routing to real multi-agent orchestration.

The methodology is under-specified in important places. The random-walk sampling procedure, seed selection, number of mutations, LLM synthesis prompts for trajectories, filtering/validation of generated data, label quality checks, candidate-pool sizes per evaluation condition, and exact inference format are insufficiently detailed for reliable reproduction.

The evaluation metric is limited to routing accuracy. There is little evidence that better routing accuracy translates into end-to-end task success, lower latency/cost, fewer execution failures, or improved real API/tool-use performance, even though the motivation is practical agent execution.

Ablations are too sparse. The only substantive ablation removes history; there is no careful isolation of graph construction, mutation operators, trajectory synthesis, synthetic-data scale, hard negatives, base model fine-tuning, or LRA design.

The comparison to large proprietary models may not be fair or informative without full prompting details, candidate serialization lengths, output parsing rules, context budgets, and cost/latency controls. Temperature 1 and avg@5 for deterministic routing are also unusual and need stronger justification.

The paper relies heavily on LLM-simulated trajectories and simulated tool results without demonstrating that these synthetic histories resemble real tool-use traces or that labels remain valid under actual API behavior.

Reproducibility is limited. No code, data release plan, benchmark split files, prompts for trajectory synthesis, or generated dataset statistics beyond a total sample count are provided in the manuscript.

Writing and presentation are polished enough to follow, but often overclaim. Terms like "universal dispatcher", "web-scale", "strong empirical foundation", and "exceptional robustness" are not warranted by the experimental design.

strengths: The paper targets a timely and relevant problem for NLP/agent systems: selecting tools or agents from large MCP-style candidate spaces under multi-turn interaction history. The motivation is clear, and the proposed router-centric framing is a useful alternative to static injection and embedding-only retrieval.

The method is coherent: candidate graph construction, mutation-based expansion, synthetic multi-turn trajectory generation, and supervised history-aware router training form a plausible pipeline for creating routing data at scale.

Empirical results are consistently positive across MCP-Universe and MCP-Mark. The 8B trained router outperforms embedding retrieval, ReAct-style routing, and strong closed-source LLM baselines, with especially strong gains on MCP-Mark and in noisy candidate settings.

The paper includes several useful analyses beyond a single leaderboard result: large candidate pool evaluation, noise robustness with both real and mutation-generated distractors, and an ablation showing that history improves routing accuracy.

The Light Routing Agent abstraction is practically appealing because it separates routing from execution and could be integrated into existing agent pipelines without injecting all tool schemas into the context.
weaknesses: The strongest claims about generalization to the broader Agent Web and universal orchestration are not fully supported. The agent-routing evaluation is self-constructed, relatively small, and appears closely aligned with the same mutation/synthesis paradigm used in training, so it is not yet strong evidence of real cross-domain generalization.

The training and evaluation depend heavily on LLM-synthesized tools, trajectories, and simulated tool results. The paper does not sufficiently validate the quality, realism, or error profile of these synthetic trajectories, making it hard to know how much of the gain transfers to real tool-use execution settings.

Reproducibility is only partial. The paper gives high-level training details and some prompts, but important details are missing or underspecified, including exact data construction settings, random-walk parameters, number and composition of noisy tools, benchmark splits, filtering criteria, and whether the generated datasets and router checkpoints will be released.

Some experimental comparisons may be unfair or underexplained. General LLM baselines are used as routers, but the exact prompts, candidate formatting, context budgets, and decoding/parsing failure handling are not described in enough detail. These choices can materially affect tool-selection accuracy.

The MCP-Mark results appear to involve small per-environment sample counts, leading to coarse 10-point accuracy jumps. The paper reports avg@5 but does not provide variance, confidence intervals, or significance tests, so the reliability of some improvements is uncertain.

The novelty is somewhat incremental: graph-based tool organization, synthetic tool-use data generation, and supervised router fine-tuning each have clear precedents. The contribution is mainly their combination for MCP routing, which is useful but not clearly transformative.

The writing occasionally overstates conclusions, using phrases such as “foundational infrastructure,” “universal dispatcher,” and “web-scale open tool ecosystems” without evidence at that scale. A more restrained framing would better match the experiments.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and relevant NLP/agent-systems problem: scalable, history-aware routing over large MCP-style tool and agent candidate spaces, where static prompt injection and embedding retrieval are plausible but limited baselines.

The proposed pipeline is coherent: candidate-graph construction, mutation-based expansion, multi-agent trajectory synthesis, and a lightweight routing wrapper form a clear training/deployment story for specialized routers.

Empirical results are directionally strong across MCP-Universe and MCP-Mark: ACE-Router outperforms embedding retrieval, ReAct, and several LLM-router baselines, with especially large gains on MCP-Mark and in noisy candidate settings.

The paper includes useful ablations showing that history and mutation both matter, plus variance over five runs and an appendix comparison against stronger retrieval baselines such as BM25, Contriever, and Qwen3-Embedding-8B.
The topic is well aligned with current computational linguistics and NLP interest in tool use, agent orchestration, and model-context protocols.
weaknesses: The main evidence is not yet strong enough for a clear Findings recommendation because the evaluation largely measures routing accuracy rather than end-to-end task success. It remains unclear how much the gains translate to successful real tool execution in realistic agent workflows.

The training/evaluation separation is insufficiently specified. The tool bank is collected from MCP-Universe and LiveMCP while MCP-Universe and MCP-Mark are used for evaluation, raising possible overlap or benchmark-specific adaptation concerns that are not ruled out.

The synthetic-data pipeline is central but under-validated. A 100-trajectory human check with Cohen’s kappa is helpful, but it does not establish correctness or diversity for the full 15k training instances, nor does it address whether LLM-simulated tool outputs induce artifacts that make routing easier than real use.

The agent-routing generalization claim is overstated. The agent benchmark is constructed by the authors from normalized and mutated agents, has only 156 samples, and appears to evaluate selection accuracy rather than multi-agent collaboration outcomes; this supports a promising transfer result, not universal Agent Web orchestration.

Reproducibility is weak: the abstract says code is available but no URL is provided, and key implementation details are missing or underspecified, including random-walk sampling parameters, mutation iteration counts, train/dev/test splits, exact prompts for trajectory generation/planning, annotation protocol, and baseline prompting.

Some baselines may be disadvantaged or not fully comparable. Embedding baselines use simple similarity, ReAct is fixed to Gemini-2.5-Pro, and LLM-router prompting/details are not described enough to judge fairness; no learned retriever or reranker baseline trained on the same data is included.

Several claims are broader than the evidence supports, especially scalability to web-scale ecosystems, robustness to massive candidate spaces, and seamless generalization from tools to agents. The experiments are encouraging but still relatively small and controlled.

Writing and presentation need polish: there are spacing/formatting issues, occasional grammatical errors, an empty code-availability field, and some tables/figures are hard to parse in text extraction, which hurts clarity.

strengths: The paper targets a timely and relevant problem: scalable, history-aware routing over large MCP/tool and agent candidate spaces, which is well aligned with current NLP/agent research.

The proposed pipeline has a coherent high-level structure: candidate graph expansion, synthetic multi-turn trajectory generation, supervised router fine-tuning, and deployment through a lightweight routing wrapper.

The experiments include several reasonable baseline families, including embedding retrieval, ReAct-style routing, and LLM router baselines, and the paper reports ablations for history and mutation as well as variance over 5 runs.

The empirical results, if taken at face value, suggest consistent gains over strong closed-source LLM routers on MCP-Universe, MCP-Mark, robustness settings, and a constructed agent-routing benchmark.
weaknesses: The central empirical claims are much stronger than the evidence supports. The paper makes broad claims about universal orchestration and Agent Web-scale generalization, but the actual evaluations are small, task-specific routing accuracy tests, with MCP-Mark results apparently based on very small per-domain sample counts.

There is a serious concern about train/evaluation separation. The router is trained using tools collected from MCP-Universe and LiveMCP and then evaluated on MCP-Universe, MCP-Mark, and tool-noise settings derived from similar sources. The paper does not clearly establish whether benchmark tools, schemas, domains, or generated trajectories leak into evaluation conditions.

The agent-routing generalization result is not convincing as an independent test. The benchmark is constructed by the authors using the same mutation and trajectory-synthesis framework as the method, contains only 156 samples, and appears to evaluate selection accuracy rather than downstream task success.

The method relies heavily on LLM-simulated trajectories and LLM-generated tool/agent mutations, but the validity check is limited to 100 synthesized trajectories and reports only agreement with human labels. This does not establish that the simulated histories correspond to realistic tool execution, useful downstream behavior, or robust supervision under real API failures.

Reproducibility is weak. The abstract says the code is available but the URL is blank, and many implementation details needed to reproduce the synthetic data pipeline are underspecified, including prompts for planning/dialogue generation, filtering criteria, exact data splits, candidate-set construction at evaluation time, decoding format, and label extraction rules.

The evaluation metric is narrow. Reporting routing accuracy alone does not show that ACE-Router improves end-to-end agent task success, latency, cost, or reliability, even though the motivation is practical agent orchestration.

Several baselines may be unfairly configured or insufficiently described. For example, embedding baselines with Q+H perform inconsistently, ReAct is reduced to a routing baseline, and LLM routers may not have access to equivalent demonstrations, candidate pruning, or fine-tuning data. The paper does not include stronger supervised retrieval/reranking baselines trained on the same synthetic data.

The presentation overstates conclusions. Terms such as “exceptional robustness,” “universal dispatcher,” and “strong empirical foundation” are not justified by the limited and partly synthetic evidence. The results are promising but not enough to support the stated scope.

Important methodological details are vague: the graph traversal procedure, mutation quality control, threshold selection, size and composition of candidate pools under each setting, and how non-callable mutated tools are handled during evaluation are not specified with enough precision.

Given the current evidence and reproducibility gaps, the paper is not yet sound enough for Findings. A revised version would need cleaner held-out evaluation, stronger independent benchmarks, public artifacts, and end-to-end task-success validation.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and relevant problem for NLP/agent systems: routing over large, dynamic MCP/tool and agent candidate spaces where static prompt injection or embedding retrieval is insufficient.

The proposed ACE-Router pipeline is coherent: graph-based candidate expansion, LLM-simulated multi-turn trajectory synthesis, history-aware router fine-tuning, and a lightweight deployment wrapper form a plausible end-to-end method.

Empirical results are consistently positive across MCP-Universe and MCP-Mark, with ACE-Router outperforming embedding retrieval, ReAct, and several strong LLM-based routers. The gains are especially notable on MCP-Mark and in noisy/expanded candidate settings.
The paper includes useful ablations showing that both history and self-evolutionary mutation contribute meaningfully, rather than attributing all gains to generic fine-tuning.

The authors make some effort toward reliability and reproducibility by reporting implementation details, 5-run variance in the appendix, mutation prompts, and a small human validation of synthesized labels with high agreement.
weaknesses: The strongest claims about generalization to the broader Agent Web are overstated relative to the evidence. The agent-routing benchmark is newly constructed, small, and closely aligned with the same synthesis/mutation paradigm, so the 91.6% result is suggestive but not yet a convincing demonstration of universal agent orchestration.

The training and evaluation setup raises possible contamination or overfitting concerns: the tool bank is drawn from MCP-Universe/LiveMCP-style sources and evaluation is on related MCP benchmarks, but the paper does not clearly separate tools, servers, domains, or candidate schemas into held-out splits.

Much of the supervision is LLM-simulated and environment-free. The human validation of 100 trajectories is helpful, but it checks only label agreement on a small sample and does not fully establish that simulated histories capture real execution failures, API behavior, or realistic multi-turn dependencies.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the abstract says code is available but the link appears missing, and key details such as trajectory synthesis prompts, sampling procedure parameters, data splits, exact candidate-pool construction, and benchmark instance construction are not fully specified in the main text.

The evaluation metric is mainly routing accuracy. The paper would be stronger with end-to-end task success, latency/cost analysis, and error analysis showing when better routing actually improves agent outcomes rather than only selecting benchmark labels.

Some baselines may not be fully comparable or optimally adapted. For example, general LLM routers and ReAct agents may be disadvantaged by prompt/candidate formatting, while stronger trained retrieval/reranking baselines are only briefly addressed in the appendix.
